title: Normal BMI, Hidden Diabetes: Why Young Indians Need Metabolic Screening
excerpt: New Indian data shows diabetes is striking people in their 20s and 30s — often slim ones. The ICMR-INDIAB study found 43.3% of adults were metabolically obese despite a normal BMI, and one in five under-30s in a 3-million-person Apollo dataset was prediabetic.
body:
• A landmark ICMR-INDIAB analysis of 113,043 adults across 31 Indian states and Union Territories found that 43.3% were "metabolically obese non-obese" — normal by standard BMI but carrying two or more metabolic risk factors. Only 26.6% were both non-obese and metabolically healthy.
  • The numbers among young Indians are stark: Apollo Hospitals’ Health of the Nation 2026 report, covering more than 3 million preventive health assessments in 2025, found that nearly half of working-age adults (average age 38) had prediabetes or diabetes, and one in five under-30s was prediabetic. The International Diabetes Federation estimated 89.8 million Indian adults had diabetes in 2024 — 43% of them, about 38.6 million people, undiagnosed.
  • What this means for you: ask your doctor for a fasting insulin test alongside fasting glucose so they can calculate your HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance — a formula combining fasting glucose and fasting insulin that flags insulin resistance years before blood sugar crosses into prediabetes). Also measure your waist: for South Asians, above 90 cm for men or 80 cm for women signals elevated metabolic risk regardless of weight.
  • India’s thresholds are stricter: the Endocrine Society of India defines overweight as BMI 23–24.9 and obesity as 25 and above. A DA-scan study of 2,347 Indian adults found critical body-fat thresholds were reached at an average BMI of just 22.

You can be 28, slim, active, and already on the road to diabetes. A convergence of new Indian data shows that lifestyle diseases long associated with middle age — type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, hypertension, and insulin resistance — are now appearing in people in their 20s and 30s, many of whom look perfectly healthy. The reason is biological, and the standard bathroom scale cannot see it.

"Only 1.8% were "metabolically healthy obese," underlining that for most people excess weight and metabolic damage travel together."

Context & Background

Researchers describe the "thin-fat" phenotype: a person may have a normal body weight while carrying excess fat around the liver, pancreas, and other internal organs. Unlike the fat stored just under the skin, this visceral fat behaves like a dysregulated gland, continually releasing inflammatory messengers and free fatty acids into the bloodstream. That impairs the body’s ability to process glucose and drives insulin resistance — the state in which cells stop responding properly to insulin even as fasting blood sugar looks normal.

South Asians are disproportionately affected. Lower skeletal muscle mass — the tissue that clears most glucose after meals — combined with a tendency to store fat internally means metabolic damage accumulates at lower body weights. South Asians also appear to have lower pancreatic beta-cell reserve, so insulin-producing cells exhaust faster under the strain of insulin resistance, accelerating the slide from prediabetes to diabetes at a younger age.

"Relying on weight alone misses the larger picture of metabolic health."

— Dr. Shashank Joshi, endocrinologist, Lilavati Hospital, Mumbai

Impact & Analysis

The ICMR-INDIAB stratification is sobering. Of the four groups studied, the largest — 43.3% — were metabolically obese despite not meeting BMI obesity thresholds, and they showed an unexpectedly elevated risk of chronic kidney disease, pronounced among women. Only 1.8% were "metabolically healthy obese," underlining that for most people excess weight and metabolic damage travel together.

Notably, the metabolically-obese-non-obese pattern was more common in rural residents (46%) than urban dwellers (39.6%) — this is not just a desk-job disease. And the burden is early: two in three young adults in the Apollo data were already at risk for non-communicable diseases, while 89.8 million Indian adults living with diabetes translates to roughly 38.6 million people walking around undiagnosed. Prediabetes is reversible. Fasting glucose of 100–125 mg/dL or HbA1c of 5.7–6.4% is a warning, not a verdict — lifestyle change at this stage can halt the progression.

Diaspora Angle

The same biology travels. South Asians in the US and UK develop type 2 diabetes nearly a decade earlier than Europeans, and clinicians abroad frequently apply Western BMI cutoffs (overweight at 25, obese at 30) that give diaspora patients false reassurance. One actionable step: at your next physical, ask your doctor to interpret your BMI against the South Asian thresholds (overweight ≥23, obesity ≥25) and to run a metabolic panel — fasting glucose, HbA1c, triglycerides, and fasting insulin for HOMA-IR — even if your weight is stable. Resistance training two to three times a week matters as much as diet here, because building muscle restores the body’s glucose-clearing capacity.

What’s Next

The clinical message is shifting from the scale to metabolic markers: waist-to-height ratio, body-composition measures, and blood work over BMI. Routine screening should stay risk-stratified — family history, waist circumference, and basic labs — rather than sending every normal-weight person for expensive scans. Crash diets are counterproductive: they burn lean muscle first, worsening the very imbalance behind the problem.

Sources: Health and Family (ICMR-INDIAB analysis), Karmactive (Apollo Health of the Nation 2026), International Diabetes Federation Diabetes Atlas
